animals.wild: Grey wolf (Canis lupus), a Late Pleistocene wolf population that is now extinct
animals.wild_look: Pack-living hunters of the Ice Age steppe-tundra, larger and stronger-jawed than most dogs; they followed the same big game as human hunters.
animals.changes: Smaller teeth and skull, shorter snout, tameness and a long puppy-like phase; later starch digestion (more AMY2B copies) and hundreds of shapes and coats.
animals.centre: Northern Eurasia, exact place unknown; Siberia proposed (Perri et al. 2021), Europe and East Asia also argued (debated)

spread.note: Natufian burial of a woman with a puppy, c. 12,000 years ago
Oldest dated dog remains in North America, c. 10,150 years ago; dogs probably came with the first Americans (debated)
Sled dogs bred for hauling c. 9,500 years ago
Oldest dingo remains, c. 3,300–3,100 years ago; dingoes came by sea from Southeast Asia
Greenland sled dogs arrive with the Inuit c. 850 years ago and stay isolated since

animals.today: Some 700 million to 1 billion dogs live worldwide, most of them free-ranging village and street dogs.
animals.fact: The dog was domesticated by Ice Age hunter-gatherers, thousands of years before anyone farmed a plant or herded a sheep.

img.shows: A pointer in a landscape, painting by George Stubbs (domestic)

img.file: File:Dogs, jackals, wolves, and foxes (Plate I).png
img.artist: J. G. Keulemans (in St. George Mivart, 1890)
img.shows: Wild grey wolf, colour plate by J. G. Keulemans in Mivart's monograph (1890)

animals.cult_note: Genetic estimates: dog lineage split from wolves 20,000–40,000 years ago; Perri et al. 2021 place domestication in Siberia c. 23,000 years ago. Older 'Palaeolithic dogs' (Goyet, Razboinichya, up to 36,000 years) are disputed. Debated.
animals.dom_note: Bonn–Oberkassel dog, buried with two humans c. 14,200 years ago, is the earliest widely accepted dog (Erralla, Spain, c. 17,500 years has also been proposed).

animals.wild: Asiatic mouflon (Ovis gmelini, syn. O. orientalis)
animals.wild_look: Short-haired, reddish-brown wild sheep of the rocky hills of Anatolia and Iran; rams carry heavy curled horns, and the coat is hair with only a short woolly undercoat that moults.
animals.changes: Smaller body and horns (many ewes hornless), floppy ears and long tails, white and spotted coats, and a fleece of continuously growing wool that must be shorn.
animals.centre: Upper Euphrates–Tigris and Zagros foothills (SE Turkey, N Iraq, W Iran)

spread.note: Sheep, goats, dogs and probably cattle and pigs shipped to Cyprus by the first farmers, c. 8800–8600 BCE
Sheep reach the Indus borderlands c. 7000 BCE (Mehrgarh dating debated; newer dates c. 5250 BCE)
Farmers bring sheep and goats into Europe
Figurines suggest selection for woolly sheep; woven wool garments by c. 4000 BCE
Sheep reach northern China c. 5,000–4,500 years ago, probably via the Hexi Corridor
Sheep arrive with the First Fleet; Australia later becomes the world's wool giant

animals.today: About 540 million sheep are slaughtered for meat each year; the living flock is about 1.2 billion (2019).
animals.fact: Early sheep were kept for meat, milk and hides; the woolly fleece only appeared thousands of years after domestication.

img.file: File:Rosa Bonheur - Sheep by the Sea (1865).jpg
img.shows: Sheep by the sea, painting by Rosa Bonheur, 1865 (domestic)
Cyprus mouflon ram, a subspecies of the wild Asiatic mouflon (it descends from early sheep taken to Cyprus and went wild)

animals.cult_note: Kill-off patterns (young males culled) in SE Anatolia and the Zagros c. 9000–8500 BCE; Wikipedia gives 11,000–9000 BC for domestication in Mesopotamia.
animals.dom_note: Larson et al. 2014: domestic sheep c. 10,500 years ago (c. 8500 BCE).

animals.wild: Bezoar ibex (Capra aegagrus), the wild goat
animals.wild_look: Agile wild goat of the cliffs of the Zagros, Taurus and Caucasus; bucks have long scimitar-shaped horns and a dark beard and shoulder stripe.
animals.changes: Smaller, with twisted or shorter horns, floppy ears and all colours; bred for milk, meat, hair (cashmere, mohair) and hardiness.
animals.centre: Zagros Mountains, western Iran (Ganj Dareh); probably several sources in the Fertile Crescent

spread.note: Goats, sheep and cattle herded at Mehrgarh (dating debated: c. 7000 or c. 5250 BCE)
Goats enter Europe with the first farmers
Goats and sheep from the Levant reach Egypt c. 6000 BCE, probably via Sinai
Herders bring goats, sheep and cattle into East Africa
Spanish conquistadors bring goats to the Americas in the 16th century

animals.today: About 1.18 billion goats lived worldwide in 2024, most in India, China and Nigeria.
animals.fact: At Ganj Dareh the herd profile shows that people culled young males 10,000 years ago, while the bones still looked fully wild.

img.shows: Goat herd grazing beside an ancient settlement mound (tell) in the Near East (domestic)
Wild bezoar goat in the Zagros Mountains, Iran

animals.cult_note: Zeder & Hesse 2000: managed goat herds (young-male cull) at Ganj Dareh c. 10,000 years ago.
animals.dom_note: Size reduction and domestic goats at Jericho, Çayönü and others c. 8,000–9,000 years ago; aDNA shows several wild source populations (Daly et al. 2018).

animals.wild: Wild boar (Sus scrofa)
animals.wild_look: Bristly dark forest pig with a long snout, tusks and striped piglets; lives in family groups and roots for food in woods and marshes.
animals.changes: Shorter snout and legs, curly tails, floppy ears, pink or spotted skin, fast growth and big litters; behaviour calmer around people.
animals.centre: Upper Tigris, SE Turkey (Çayönü); a second, independent centre in China

spread.note: Pigs domesticated independently from East Asian wild boar c. 8,000 years ago (second centre)
Near Eastern pigs reach Europe at least 8,500 years ago, then mix with local wild boar
Austronesian seafarers carry pigs, chickens and dogs into the Pacific
Polynesians bring pigs to Hawaii
Columbus's second voyage lands pigs in the Americas

animals.today: About 1 billion domestic pigs live today; China produces nearly half of the world’s pork.
animals.fact: European pigs kept their domestic looks but today carry less than 5% Near Eastern DNA, because they interbred with local wild boar for 3,000 years.

img.file: File:Paulus Potter - A Landscape with a Herd of Pigs, The Swineherd Conversing with Another Man - 2017.48 - Minneapolis Institute of Art.jpg
img.shows: Herd of pigs with swineherds in a landscape, painting by Paulus Potter (domestic)
Wild boar in its forest habitat

animals.cult_note: Wild boar shipped to Cyprus more than 11,400 years ago, implying management on the mainland (Vigne et al.).
animals.dom_note: Larson et al. 2014: domestic pigs c. 10,500 years ago in SW Asia (Çayönü); China c. 8,000 years ago.

animals.wild: Aurochs (Bos primigenius), extinct since 1627
animals.wild_look: Huge wild ox, bulls up to 1.8 m at the shoulder, black with a pale back stripe and long forward-curving horns; lived in open woods and river valleys across Eurasia and North Africa.
animals.changes: Much smaller and calmer, many coat colours, smaller horns (or none); later bred for milk, meat and pulling ploughs and carts.
animals.centre: Upper Euphrates and Tigris valleys (N Syria, SE Turkey; Dja'de, Çayönü)

spread.note: Early farmers ship cattle to Cyprus by boat (Shillourokambos); they die out there in the 8th millennium BCE
Cattle enter Europe with the first farmers
Linear Pottery farmers keep cattle across central Europe
Cattle herders in a green Sahara; claims of a separate African domestication c. 8000 BCE (Nabta Playa) are debated
Cattle arrive with Neolithic farmers
Columbus's second voyage brings cattle to the Americas

animals.today: Over 940 million cattle were counted in 2022 (taurine and zebu together).
animals.fact: All taurine cattle may descend from only about 80 wild aurochs cows captured in the Near East.

img.shows: The Young Bull, painting by Paulus Potter (domestic)
Wild aurochs, painting by Heinrich Harder (c. 1920)

animals.cult_note: Size change and management of aurochs at Dja'de el-Mughara and Çayönü c. 8800–8300 BCE (Helmer et al.).
animals.dom_note: Wikipedia: taurine cattle domesticated c. 10,500 years ago in Anatolia, the Levant and W Iran; Bollongino et al. 2012: c. 80 founding cows.

animals.wild: Indian aurochs (Bos primigenius namadicus), extinct
animals.wild_look: South Asian form of the aurochs, a huge wild ox of the Indian plains; its last remains date to about 3,800 years ago.
animals.changes: Shoulder hump, big dewlap and drooping ears, loose skin; tolerant of heat, drought and ticks.
animals.centre: Mehrgarh, Baluchistan (Pakistan)

spread.note: Humped bulls on Harappan seals
Zebu bulls spread west and mix with taurine cattle during the 4.2-ka drought (Verdugo et al. 2019)
Zebu reaches the Horn c. 1000 CE and the rest of sub-Saharan Africa after 700 CE (Zebu article); arrival in East Africa 3,500–2,500 years ago is also proposed (debated)
Indian zebu breeds imported; Nelore type now dominates Brazilian beef

animals.today: Zebu and zebu-cross cattle make up most of the herds of India, Africa and tropical South America; India alone had 65.7 million draft cattle in 1998.
animals.fact: More than 80% of Brazil’s beef cattle are Nelore or Nelore crosses, descended from Ongole cattle of southern India.

img.shows: Zebu cattle at a market in Madagascar (domestic)

animals.cult_note: Cattle bones at Mehrgarh from the 7th millennium BCE; size decrease of local cattle (Meadow).
animals.dom_note: Larson et al. 2014: zebu c. 8,000 years ago; Wikipedia Zebu gives 6,000–7,000 years ago at Mehrgarh (estimates differ).

animals.wild: Wild water buffalo (Bubalus arnee)
animals.wild_look: Massive grey-black wild ox of swamps and river floodplains of India and Southeast Asia, with very wide sweeping horns; spends hot hours wallowing in mud.
animals.changes: Calmer and smaller-horned; two types: river buffalo (India, bred for milk) and swamp buffalo (SE Asia, ploughing paddies), domesticated separately.
animals.centre: River buffalo: western India; swamp buffalo: mainland Southeast Asia (separate domestication)

spread.note: Water buffalo shown on Akkadian cylinder seals, brought from the Indus
Swamp buffalo in mainland Southeast Asia, domesticated separately 3,000–7,000 years ago
Butchered domestic buffalo at Nagsabaran, at least 2,500 years ago
River buffalo reach southern Italy in the early Middle Ages (perhaps via Arab Sicily; origin debated); buffalo-milk cheeses recorded from the 12th century

animals.today: About 208 million water buffalo live in 77 countries and give 72 million tonnes of milk a year.
animals.fact: River and swamp buffalo have different numbers of chromosomes (50 and 48); they do not readily interbreed, yet their hybrids can be fertile.

img.shows: Child ploughing with a swamp buffalo in Laos (domestic)

img.file: File:Wild water buffalo at Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve.jpg
img.shows: Wild water buffalo at Koshi Tappu, Nepal

animals.cult_note: Phylogenetic estimate: river buffalo domesticated in western India c. 6,300 years ago (c. 4300 BCE); genetic, not archaeological.
animals.dom_note: Water buffalo on Indus (Harappan) seals c. 2500 BCE; swamp buffalo separately in SE Asia.

animals.wild: African wildcat (Felis lybica), Near Eastern and North African form
animals.wild_look: Sandy-grey, faintly striped wildcat with long legs and a ringed tail; a solitary hunter of rodents in dry scrub and around villages.
animals.changes: Hardly changed in body: tamer, smaller brain, more coat colours and patterns (tabby blotches, white, ginger); they largely domesticated themselves by hunting mice in grain stores.
animals.centre: Near East / Fertile Crescent, later Egypt

spread.note: A tomb painting of Baqet III (11th Dynasty) shows a cat facing a rodent; Egypt’s cats later spread around the Mediterranean
Earliest domestic cat in Greece c. 1200 BCE
Domestic cats spread through Europe with Roman trade, c. 2,000 years ago
Egyptian cat lineage reaches a Baltic port by the end of the Western Roman Empire
Domestic cats reach China along the Silk Roads (earlier Chinese 'cats' were tamed leopard cats)

animals.today: An estimated 600 million domestic cats live worldwide, 400 million of them in Asia.
animals.fact: A cat buried beside a person at Shillourokambos, Cyprus, c. 7500 BCE must have been brought by boat, because Cyprus had no wildcats.

img.shows: Wild African wildcat (Sardinian population) in Mediterranean scrub
Domestic cat

animals.cult_note: Shillourokambos, Cyprus, c. 7500–7200 BCE: wildcat buried near a human grave (taming, not necessarily domestication). Debated.
animals.dom_note: Cats in Egyptian Middle Kingdom art c. 1950 BCE; Ottoni et al. 2017 aDNA: Near Eastern and Egyptian lineages. When cats became fully domestic is debated.

animals.wild: Red junglefowl (Gallus gallus), mainly the subspecies G. g. spadiceus
animals.wild_look: Shy, slender forest-edge bird of Southeast Asia; cocks have red combs, golden hackles and green-black tails, hens are brown; flies well.
animals.changes: Larger and heavier, lays eggs all year (a junglefowl hen lays only a few clutches), many plumage colours, many no longer fly.
animals.centre: Mainland Southeast Asia (central Thailand; Ban Non Wat)

spread.note: Chickens reach the Mediterranean c. 800 BCE, first as exotic birds
Lapita seafarers carry chickens into Remote Oceania
Polynesians bring chickens to Hawaii
European ships bring chickens; pre-Columbian chickens in Chile are debated

animals.today: About 74 billion chickens are slaughtered for meat every year, by far the most numerous farm animal.
animals.fact: For centuries after reaching Europe, chickens were kept for cockfighting and as sacred birds, not for eggs or meat.

img.file: File:Feeding the chickens, by Walter Frederick Osborne.jpg
img.shows: Feeding the chickens, painting by Walter Osborne (domestic)
Wild red junglefowl cock at Kaeng Krachan, Thailand

animals.cult_note: Peters et al. 2022 (PNAS): earliest probable chicken bones at Ban Non Wat, central Thailand, c. 1650–1250 BCE, tied to rice and millet farming.
animals.dom_note: Same evidence; genomic estimates (up to 8,000 years ago) and older claims from China are debated.

animals.wild: Wild horse (Equus ferus) of the western Eurasian steppe; the European tarpan survived to the 19th century
animals.wild_look: Stocky dun wild horse with a big head and upright mane, living in herds on the steppe and hunted by Ice Age people.
animals.changes: Calmer temperament and a stronger back for riding (genes GSDMC and ZFPM1 selected, Librado 2021); later all sizes, coat colours and gaits.
animals.centre: Lower Volga–Don, Pontic–Caspian steppe (aDNA: DOM2 lineage)

spread.note: Spoke-wheeled chariots and horse burials c. 2000 BCE
DOM2 horses spread across Eurasia within a few centuries, replacing other horses
Horses and chariots arrive in the Hyksos period
Shang-dynasty chariot burials
Columbus's second voyage brings horses back to the Americas, where native horses had died out c. 10,000 years earlier
Horses arrive with the First Fleet

animals.today: An estimated 100 million horses, donkeys and mules still work in agriculture and transport.
animals.fact: The famous Botai horses of Kazakhstan turned out to be ancestors of Przewalski's horses, not of today's domestic horses.

img.shows: The Horse Fair, painting by Rosa Bonheur, 1852–55 (domestic)

img.file: File:Charles Hamilton Smith - The Tarpan Wild Horse Native to Russia - B1981.25.2215 - Yale Center for British Art.jpg
img.shows: Wild tarpan horse of the Russian steppe, watercolour by Charles Hamilton Smith

animals.cult_note: Botai culture, Kazakhstan, 3700–3500 BCE: possible bit wear and horse milk; aDNA (Gaunitz 2018) shows these horses fed into Przewalski's horses; management vs. domestication is debated.
animals.dom_note: Librado et al. 2021 (Nature): DOM2 horses arose in the Volga–Don region c. 2200 BCE and spread rapidly with chariots.

animals.wild: African wild ass (Equus africanus), Nubian and probably other now-lost populations
animals.wild_look: Grey desert ass with long ears, a dark shoulder cross and zebra-striped legs (Somali form); survives on little water in rocky deserts of NE Africa.
animals.changes: Calm, sure-footed pack and riding animal; varied size and colour; wild ass now critically endangered.
animals.centre: East Africa / Horn of Africa (genomics, Todd et al. 2022)

spread.note: Ten donkeys buried beside an early pharaoh's tomb, with backs worn by loads
Donkeys carry loads across the Near East; kunga hybrids (donkey × Syrian wild ass) pull Sumerian war wagons, c. 2600–2000 BCE
First donkeys in the Americas, from Columbus's second voyage
Pack donkeys imported; up to 5 million feral donkeys today

animals.today: Almost 54 million donkeys lived worldwide in 2024, most in Ethiopia and other African countries.
animals.fact: The donkey is the only major livestock animal domesticated in Africa from a wild animal of Africa (cattle there came from the Near East).

img.file: File:Paulus Potter - Spring Landscape with Donkeys and Goats 6688.jpg
img.shows: Donkeys and goats in a spring landscape, painting by Paulus Potter (domestic)
Wild African wild ass (Somali form), St. Louis Zoo

animals.cult_note: Todd et al. 2022 (Science): genomes point to a single domestication in East Africa c. 5000 BCE (estimate).
animals.dom_note: Abydos donkey burials c. 3000 BCE (Rossel et al. 2008); Wikipedia: domesticated 5,000–7,000 years ago.

animals.wild: Wild dromedary, extinct (hunted in Arabia until c. 1000 BCE)
animals.wild_look: One-humped wild camel of the Arabian coasts and deserts, known only from bones and rock art; hunted for meat by Neolithic Arabians.
animals.changes: Tame load-carrier and milk animal able to cross deserts for weeks; still interbreeds little with other camels.
animals.centre: South-east Arabian Peninsula

spread.note: Earliest domestic camels in the southern Levant, at copper mines c. 930 BCE
Dromedaries are in use south of the Sahara, in the Senegal valley, by the 3rd century CE; later they carry trans-Saharan trade
Dromedaries introduced to Spain
Dromedaries imported for desert exploration; today the world's largest feral herd

animals.today: FAO counted about 10 million dromedaries in eastern Africa alone already in 1984; Somalia and Sudan hold the biggest herds.
animals.fact: The only wild dromedaries left are feral, mainly in Australia, descended from 19th-century imports.

img.shows: Domestic dromedary in the Sahara near Merzouga, Morocco
Woman milking a dromedary in Niger (domestic)

animals.cult_note: Wikipedia: first domesticated in southern Arabia c. 4000–3000 BC (early, wild-or-tame camel bones are hard to tell apart).
animals.dom_note: Almathen et al. 2016: domestic camels in SE Arabia by c. 3,000 years ago; clear domestic remains from the end of the 2nd millennium BCE (estimate).

animals.wild: An extinct wild two-humped camel of Central Asia (the living wild Bactrian camel, C. ferus, is a separate species, not the ancestor)
animals.wild_look: Shaggy two-humped camel of cold Central Asian deserts and steppes, able to drink brackish water and survive harsh winters.
animals.changes: Tame pack and riding animal for the Silk Roads; thick moulting wool; larger and calmer than its wild relatives.
animals.centre: Central Asia, probably NE Iran / Turkmenistan

spread.note: Early domestic Bactrian camels at the Bronze Age ‘Burnt City’, c. 2500 BCE
Assyrian kings receive Bactrian camels as tribute from Median lands; the camels spread to the Near East during the 2nd millennium BCE
Camel saddles appear by c. 1200 BCE; Bactrian camels become riding and pack animals of the steppe
Caravans of Bactrian camels link China and the West

animals.today: About 2 million Bactrian camels live, almost all domestic, across the cold deserts and steppes of Central Asia, Mongolia and China.
animals.fact: The truly wild Bactrian camel of the Gobi split from the domestic camel’s ancestors some 0.7–1.1 million years ago; only about 1,000 survive.

img.shows: Domestic Bactrian camels in western Mongolia

img.file: File:Wild Bactrian camel on road east of Yarkand.jpg
img.shows: Bactrian camel near Yarkand, Xinjiang (described as wild; the wild species is a relative, not the ancestor)

animals.cult_note: Estimate from Bronze Age Central Asian sites, c. 3000 BCE (approximate).
animals.dom_note: Wikipedia: Bactrian camel domesticated c. 2500 BCE.

animals.wild: Guanaco (Lama guanicoe)
animals.wild_look: Slender, reddish-brown wild camelid of Andean grasslands and Patagonian steppe, living in herds led by a territorial male.
animals.changes: Larger and stronger pack animal, many coat colours, coarse wool; carries 25–30 kg over mountain trails.
animals.centre: Central Andes puna, Peru (Junín; Telarmachay)

spread.note: The Moche bury llamas with important people and model them realistically in pottery
Llamas are the only beasts of burden of the Inca Empire
Up to 300,000 llamas haul produce from the Potosí mines (Spanish estimate)
First llamas imported to the US as zoo animals in the late 1800s; herds grow from the late 20th century

animals.today: Over 7 million llamas and alpacas lived in South America in 2007.
animals.fact: One scholar argues that Andean farming only became possible because llama dung was used as fertilizer (Chepstow-Lusty; debated).

img.file: File:Llamas, Laguna Milluni y Nevado Huayna Potosí (La Paz - Bolivia).jpg
img.shows: Llamas below Huayna Potosí in the Bolivian Andes (domestic)
Wild guanaco at Torres del Paine, Chile

animals.cult_note: Shift from hunting to herding of camelids at Telarmachay and Junín c. 6,000–7,000 years ago (Wheeler).
animals.dom_note: Llama and alpaca domesticated at least 5,000–6,000 years ago (Wikipedia; Larson et al. 2014).

animals.wild: Vicuña (Vicugna vicugna)
animals.wild_look: Small, graceful, cinnamon-coloured camelid of the high puna above 3,500 m, with extremely fine wool.
animals.changes: Larger, with much more and longer fine wool in many colours; bred for fibre rather than loads.
animals.centre: Central Andes puna, Peru (Junín; Telarmachay)

spread.note: Mummified llamas and alpacas of two breeds, c. 900–1000 years old
Alpaca wool for fine textiles of the Inca state
Charles Ledger lands 256 alpacas, llamas and vicuñas in Sydney after driving them across the Andes to Chile; the flock later dwindled
Alpacas reach North America in 1984 and are now farmed worldwide

animals.today: Over 7 million llamas and alpacas lived in South America in 2007, most alpacas in Peru.
animals.fact: After the Spanish conquest of 1532 about 98% of alpacas were destroyed; the survivors were pushed into the high Andes.

img.shows: Alpacas in Ecuador (domestic)

img.file: File:Group of vicuña in Arequipa Region, Peru.jpg
img.shows: Wild vicuñas in the Arequipa region, Peru

animals.cult_note: Shift from hunting to herding of camelids at Telarmachay and Junín c. 6,000–7,000 years ago (Wheeler).
animals.dom_note: Llama and alpaca domesticated at least 5,000–6,000 years ago (Wikipedia; DNA shows the vicuña as alpaca ancestor, Kadwell et al. 2001).

animals.wild: Montane guinea pig (Cavia tschudii)
animals.wild_look: Small brown, grass-eating cavy of Andean valleys and grasslands, living in groups under shrubs and rocks.
animals.changes: Larger and heavier, many coat colours and long-haired forms, calmer; bred as food and ritual animal, kept in homes.
animals.centre: Andes of southern Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia

spread.note: Ceramic-making migrants bring guinea pigs to the West Indies
Conrad Gessner describes the guinea pig, newly brought from South America
Earliest European painting of a pet guinea pig
Dutch traders bring guinea pigs to Japan

animals.today: Peruvians eat an estimated 65 million guinea pigs (cuy) each year.
animals.fact: An Elizabethan portrait of c. 1580 shows a girl holding a tortoiseshell guinea pig, only decades after Europeans first saw one.

img.shows: Three Elizabethan children, one holding a pet guinea pig, painting c. 1580 (domestic)
Wild montane guinea pig

animals.cult_note: Wikipedia: first domesticated as early as 5000 BC in the Andes (estimate).
animals.dom_note: Same estimate; selective breeding of many varieties c. 1200–1532 CE. The early date is uncertain.

animals.wild: Wild turkey (Meleagris gallopavo), south Mexican subspecies M. g. gallopavo
animals.wild_look: Large, bronze-green woodland bird of North American forests; flies short distances and roosts in trees.
animals.changes: Heavier, slower, many cannot fly or breed naturally; white feathers in most modern breeds.
animals.centre: Central and southern Mexico (Mesoamerica); a separate domestication among the Ancestral Puebloans in the US Southwest

spread.note: Mexican turkeys traded far outside their wild range, 300 BCE–100 CE
Turkeys kept for feathers, separate domestication (Speller et al. 2010)
Spaniards bring domestic turkeys from Mexico to Europe
The navigator William Strickland is credited with bringing turkeys to England; by 1573 they are Christmas fare
European domestic turkeys shipped back to North America

animals.today: About 620 million turkeys are slaughtered for meat each year.
animals.fact: Domestic turkeys descend from Mexican birds; some went to Europe and were shipped back across the Atlantic to Jamestown in 1608.

img.shows: Black Spanish turkeys, an old domestic breed
Wild turkey, plate by John James Audubon, Birds of America

animals.cult_note: Thornton et al. 2012: south-Mexican turkeys at El Mirador, Guatemala, 300 BCE–100 CE, outside their wild range.
animals.dom_note: Wikipedia: domesticated in Mesoamerica at least 2,000 years ago (estimate; 2,200–2,700 years in 'Domestication of animals').

animals.wild: Wild Muscovy duck (Cairina moschata)
animals.wild_look: Large, black, glossy-green duck of tropical South and Central American forest rivers; perches and nests in trees.
animals.changes: Heavier, often white or pied, larger red face caruncles; quiet and tame.
animals.centre: Northern South America

spread.note: Kept by many South American peoples before 1492
Brought to Europe in the 16th century; the 'Muscovy' name is unexplained

animals.today: Muscovy ducks and the mule-duck hybrids bred from them supply much of France's duck meat and foie gras.
animals.fact: Despite its name, the Muscovy duck has nothing to do with Moscow; it is one of only two birds domesticated in the Americas.

img.shows: Domestic Muscovy ducks (canards de Barbarie)
Wild Muscovy drake in the Pantanal, Brazil

animals.cult_note: Wikipedia 'Domestication of animals': domesticated as early as 50 CE (estimate, poorly dated).
animals.dom_note: Same; archaeological record is thin (estimate).

animals.wild: Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos)
animals.wild_look: Common wild dabbling duck of wetlands across the Northern Hemisphere; drakes have glossy green heads; strong flyers and migrants.
animals.changes: Heavier, many lay far more eggs, white or varied plumage, upright 'runner' forms; most cannot fly well.
animals.centre: Southern China (rice-paddy farmers)

spread.note: Rice farmers of southern China domesticate ducks c. 2000 BCE (few finds; date uncertain) and spread them outward
Romans keep ducks in netted pens (nessotrophia), raised from wild-caught eggs rather than bred
Pekin ducks shipped from China reach New York; Long Island becomes the centre of US duck farming

animals.today: About 4.3 billion ducks were slaughtered in 2021, over 80% of them in China.
animals.fact: In rice–duck farming in East and Southeast Asia, ducks eat pests and weeds in the paddy and manure the rice, so one field yields both.

img.shows: Indian Runner ducks, an upright domestic breed

img.file: File:Ferdinand von Wright - Mallards - A-2002-608 - Finnish National Gallery.jpg
img.shows: Wild mallards, painting by Ferdinand von Wright

animals.cult_note: Wikipedia: mallard domesticated in southern China around 2000 BC (estimate).
animals.dom_note: Same estimate.

animals.sci: Anser cygnoides domesticus and Anser anser domesticus
animals.wild: Swan goose (Anser cygnoides) in East Asia; greylag goose (Anser anser) in Europe and the Near East
animals.wild_look: Large grey wild geese of marshes and lakes, grazing grass in flocks and migrating in V-shaped skeins.
animals.changes: Heavier and flightless, white or pied forms; Chinese geese keep a knob on the bill; good guards and egg layers.
animals.centre: Lower Yangtze, China (Tianluoshan, Hemudu culture)

spread.note: Geese kept in Egypt over 4,000 years ago; fully domestic by the New Kingdom
Domestic geese in Homer's Odyssey
Sacred geese of Juno said to have warned Rome of the Gallic attack (legend)
Domestic geese reach Scandinavia in the Early Iron Age

animals.today: About 750 million geese are slaughtered for meat each year.
animals.fact: The domestic geese of China and of Europe come from two different wild species, yet they interbreed freely.

img.shows: Geese at the village pond, painting by Hermann Baisch (domestic)

animals.wild: Wild yak (Bos mutus)
animals.wild_look: Huge black wild ox of the high Tibetan Plateau with a long shaggy skirt of hair, living above 4,000 m.
animals.changes: Smaller, often pied or white, calmer; gives milk, butter, wool and dung fuel, and carries loads at extreme altitude.
animals.centre: Tibetan Plateau (Qinghai)
animals.today: Domestic yaks live across the Himalaya, the Tibetan Plateau and the Pamirs and north into Mongolia and Siberia; their dried dung is often the only fuel on the treeless plateau.
animals.fact: Wild yak bulls can weigh a tonne, about twice as much as domestic yaks.

img.shows: Domestic yak herd in Muguthang valley, Sikkim

animals.cult_note: Qiu et al. 2015: genomic estimate of domestication c. 7,300 years ago (genetic only, debated).
animals.dom_note: Wikipedia: oldest dated physical evidence of yak domestication c. 2,500 years ago.

animals.wild: Wild reindeer / caribou (Rangifer tarandus)
animals.wild_look: Antlered deer of tundra and taiga, both sexes antlered; migrates in huge herds and digs lichen from under snow.
animals.changes: Only semi-domesticated: tamer, often lighter or spotted, used for milk, meat, riding and pulling sleds; still mixes with wild herds.
animals.centre: Sayan Mountains, S Siberia (rock art, proposed; debated)

spread.note: Harness pieces and draught-worn bones of reindeer, c. 2,000 years ago (Losey et al. 2021)
Ohthere tells King Alfred he owns 600 tame reindeer
Mountain Sámi take up the semi-nomadic reindeer-herding way of life from around 1500
Reindeer brought from Siberia for Alaska Natives

animals.today: About 100,000 people herd reindeer across the circumpolar north.
animals.fact: The reindeer is the only deer semi-domesticated on a large scale, and herders still let many of their animals roam half-wild.

img.shows: Reindeer near Lake Khövsgöl, Mongolia (herded)

animals.cult_note: Wikipedia: rock art suggests first domestication in the Sayan Mountains, 2–3 thousand years ago (debated).
animals.dom_note: Losey et al. 2021: reindeer used for draught at Ust-Polui, Yamal, c. 2,000 years ago (debated).

animals.wild: Wild colonies of the same species (honey bees were never fully domesticated)
animals.wild_look: Colonies of tens of thousands of bees nesting in hollow trees and rock crevices across Africa, Europe and western Asia.
animals.changes: Little genetic change: people supply hives and select calmer, productive colonies; bees still swarm and go wild easily.
animals.centre: Nile valley, Egypt (earliest hives in art)

spread.note: An apiary of about 100 clay hives, c. 900 BCE
Honey bees shipped to the English colony
First honey bees arrive
Honey bees introduced

animals.today: The world had about 83 million managed beehives in 2014 (FAO).
animals.fact: People took wild honey long before any hive: Spanish rock paintings about 8,000 years old show honey collecting.

img.shows: The Beekeepers, drawing by Pieter Bruegel the Elder (managed hives)

animals.cult_note: Beeswax residues in Near Eastern pottery from c. 7000 BCE (Roffet-Salque et al. 2015) - exploitation, not necessarily hives.
animals.dom_note: Beekeeping scenes (smoke at hives) in the sun temple of Nyuserre, Egypt, before 2422 BCE.

animals.wild: Wild silk moth (Bombyx mandarina)
animals.wild_look: Brown moth of East Asia whose caterpillars feed on wild mulberry; adults fly well and caterpillars are camouflaged.
animals.changes: Completely dependent on people: moths are white, cannot fly, caterpillars do not wander, and cocoons are bigger.
animals.centre: Yellow River / Yangtze, China (Yangshao and Liangzhu cultures)

spread.note: Sericulture reaches Khotan c. 50 CE (legend: a Chinese princess hid silkworms in her hair)
Monks smuggle silkworm eggs to the Byzantine Empire for Justinian I (c. 553–54)
Roger II brings Greek silk weavers to Palermo
Francis I grants Lyon’s silk weavers royal privileges; Lyon becomes Europe’s silk capital

animals.today: One cocoon yields about 900 m of silk filament.
animals.fact: The domestic silk moth cannot fly; males even need human help to find a mate, and it no longer lives in the wild.

Wild silk moth (Bombyx mandarina), Taiwan

animals.cult_note: Silkworm-shaped ceramic from Nancun, Hebei, 5,400–5,500 years ago; earlier silk residues at Jiahu (c. 6500 BCE) are debated.
animals.dom_note: Silk fabric of domesticated silkworms at Qianshanyang, Zhejiang, c. 2700 BCE (Liangzhu); Confucian tradition also gives c. 2700 BCE.

animals.wild: European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus), originally only in Iberia and southern France
animals.wild_look: Small grey-brown rabbit living in colonies in burrow systems (warrens) in the dry scrub of Iberia.
animals.changes: Larger and smaller breeds, lop ears, many colours and long fur (angora); tame, breeds year-round in hutches.
animals.centre: Southern France (medieval monasteries); wild rabbits from Iberia

spread.note: Romans keep rabbits in walled leporaria and spread them around the Mediterranean
Normans bring rabbits for warrens; they become established in the 12th–13th centuries (Lundy: 2,000 caught a year by 1274)
Thomas Austin releases 24 wild rabbits; they spread across the continent
Rabbits released on the mainland (Blenheim 1858, 1865) become one of the worst pests

animals.today: Rabbits are farmed for meat and fur worldwide and are among the most popular pets.
animals.fact: The tale that monks domesticated rabbits c. 600 CE because unborn rabbits counted as 'fish' at Lent is a myth (Irving-Pease et al. 2018).

img.shows: Flemish Giant, a large domestic rabbit breed
Wild European rabbit in Beja, Portugal

animals.cult_note: Roman authors (Varro, Pliny) describe rabbits kept in walled enclosures; captive rabbits exploited for over 2,000 years (Wikipedia).
animals.dom_note: Monks in southern France were crossbreeding rabbits at least by the 12th century; clear skeletal differences only from the 1800s. Gradual process (Irving-Pease et al. 2018).

animals.wild: European polecat (Mustela putorius), possibly with steppe polecat
animals.wild_look: Dark-brown, masked wild weasel of European woods and farmland, hunting rabbits, rodents and frogs at night.
animals.changes: Tamer, often albino or pale, depends on people; used to drive rabbits from burrows and to kill rats.
animals.centre: Mediterranean (probably Iberia / North Africa)

spread.note: Augustus sends ‘viverrae’ from Libya against the Balearic rabbit plague (Strabo, Pliny); possibly ferrets (debated)
An English law of 1390 restricts hunting with ferrets to the well-off
Ferrets reach the Americas in the 17th century
Ferrets imported from 1879 and some 4,000 released in 1884–86 to control rabbits; they turned to native birds

animals.today: Over five million pet ferrets live in the United States alone.
animals.fact: Ferrets were released in New Zealand to kill the introduced rabbits, and instead began eating native birds.

Wild European polecat, painting by Archibald Thorburn

animals.cult_note: mtDNA estimate: ferrets domesticated c. 2,500 years ago (Wikipedia).
animals.dom_note: Same; ancient texts confirm use against rabbits by Roman times.

tips.t: In the Zagros and upper Euphrates hunters began sparing female goats, sheep and aurochs and culling young males. Bones still looked wild for centuries, but the herd profile shows herding.
tips.step_hint: first herders in the Zagros, c. 8000 BCE

tips.t: Early farmers shipped sheep, goats, pigs, cattle and even a cat to Cyprus, an island with none of them. Domestic animals travelled with people from the start.
Thousands of years after domestication, people learned to use living animals: milk, wool, ploughing and carts. Wool sheep and milking spread across Eurasia in the 4th millennium BCE.
tips.step_hint: secondary products and the plough, c. 4000–3500 BCE

tips.t: In the high Andes, llamas, alpacas and guinea pigs were domesticated independently of the Old World; llama dung fuelled and fertilised life above 4,000 m.
tips.step_hint: Andean farming and herding, c. 4000 BCE

notes: Dates are signed years (BCE negative). 'cult' = earliest evidence of management or close association; 'dom' = earliest clear domestic form (morphology, genetics or depictions). Domestication was a slow process, so both dates are approximate; genetic clock estimates are estimates, not observations. Debated: dog origin place and age (Siberia vs Europe vs East Asia; 'Palaeolithic dogs'); horse at Botai (managed wild horses, ancestors of Przewalski's horse, not DOM2); cat at Shillourokambos (tamed, not proven domestic) and when cats became fully domestic; chicken age (Ban Non Wat c. 1650 BCE vs older genomic estimates); African cattle domestication at Nabta Playa; yak (genetic 7,300 years vs physical 2,500 years); reindeer (only semi-domestic, place uncertain); goose (China vs Egypt/Europe); guinea pig and Muscovy duck dates are poorly constrained. Honey bee is managed rather than domesticated. Pig and goose/water buffalo have two centres; the main centre is in 'centre', the second appears in a spread entry or the 'centre' text. Living wild Bactrian camels and Przewalski's horses are relatives, not ancestors. Present-day numbers are from Wikipedia/FAO and differ by year and source. Images verified on Wikimedia Commons (licence and artist from Commons metadata, 2026-10-14).
